guide.summary: Momentum describes how hard it is to stop a moving object, and it is conserved whenever a system has no net external force. This unit covers momentum and impulse, the impulse-momentum theorem, conservation in collisions and explosions, the difference between elastic and inelastic collisions, and center-of-mass velocity.

sections.heading: Momentum and impulse
sections.body:
Momentum is a vector:

p = mv

measured in kg·m/s. Direction matters: pick a positive direction and keep signs consistent.

**Impulse** is the effect of a force over time:

J = F_avg·Δt = area under a force-versus-time graph

The **impulse-momentum theorem**:

J = Δp

This explains safety design. Airbags, crumple zones, and bending your knees when you land all increase Δt for the same Δp, which lowers the average force.

Watch signs on bounces. A 0.2 kg ball hitting a wall at 10 m/s and rebounding at 10 m/s has Δp = 0.2(−10) − 0.2(10) = −4 kg·m/s, magnitude 4, not zero. Bouncing transfers more momentum than stopping.

sections.heading: Conservation of momentum
sections.body:
If the net external force on a system is zero (or its impulse is negligible during a brief collision), the system's total momentum is constant:

m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′

Internal forces, like the forces two colliding carts exert on each other, are equal and opposite by Newton's third law, so they cancel within the system.

**Explosions and recoil** start with zero momentum. A 60 kg skater at rest on frictionless ice throws a 2 kg ball at 15 m/s; the skater recoils at (2 × 15)/60 = 0.5 m/s in the opposite direction.

sections.heading: Types of collisions
sections.body:
| Collision | Momentum | Kinetic energy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Elastic | conserved | conserved |
| Inelastic | conserved | decreases |
| Perfectly inelastic (stick together) | conserved | maximum possible decrease |

Momentum is conserved in all three (if the system is isolated). Kinetic energy is lost to internal energy, sound, and deformation in inelastic collisions.

Example: a 2 kg cart at 6 m/s hits a 4 kg cart at rest and they stick. Momentum: 12 = 6v, so v = 2 m/s. Kinetic energy before: 36 J; after: 12 J; 24 J was converted.

In a 1D elastic collision between equal masses with one at rest, the moving object stops and the other leaves with the original velocity.

sections.heading: Center of mass
sections.body:
A system's center of mass moves as if all the mass were there and all external forces acted on it. Its velocity is

v_cm = (m₁v₁ + m₂v₂)/(m₁ + m₂) = p_total/m_total

With no net external force, v_cm is constant, before, during, and after any collision or explosion. For a 2 kg object at 3 m/s right and a 1 kg object at 3 m/s left, v_cm = (6 − 3)/3 = 1 m/s right, no matter what happens when they collide.

sections.heading: Experimental work
sections.body: Momentum labs typically use carts on a low-friction track with motion sensors or photogates. To test conservation, measure masses with a balance and velocities before and after, then compare total momentum. Plotting p_after versus p_before for many trials gives a line whose slope should be close to 1. Friction on the track is a small external force, so p_after is usually slightly less than p_before.

keyTakeaways: p = mv is a vector; signs matter.
J = FΔt = Δp; impulse is the area under F–t.
Momentum is conserved when net external force (impulse) is zero.
All isolated collisions conserve momentum; only elastic ones conserve kinetic energy.
Longer collision time means smaller average force for the same Δp.
Center-of-mass velocity is constant without external force.
commonMistakes: Ignoring direction, especially in bounces and explosions.
Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in every collision.
Saying an airbag reduces impulse; it reduces the force by increasing time.
Forgetting that objects that stick together share one final velocity.
Calling momentum conserved when an external force (like friction over a long time) acts.
Confusing impulse units (N·s) with work units (J).
examTips: Define the system and justify conservation: "no net external force acts horizontally."
In LAB questions, describe measurements with specific equipment and repeated trials.
When graphing p_after vs p_before, the slope tests conservation; discuss deviations with a physical cause.
Check kinetic energy before and after to classify a collision.
Use force-time graph areas for impulse; mind units (N·s = kg·m/s).
guide.cramSheet:
**Momentum:** p = mv (vector)

**Impulse:** J = FΔt = area under F–t = Δp

**Conservation:** Σp_before = Σp_after if F_net,ext = 0

**Collisions:** elastic (K conserved) · inelastic (K lost) · perfectly inelastic (stick)

**Stick:** v_f = (m₁v₁ + m₂v₂)/(m₁ + m₂)

**Recoil:** m₁v₁ = −m₂v₂ from rest

**v_cm:** p_total/m_total, constant if isolated

**Bounce:** Δp larger than stopping

vocab.definition: The product of mass and velocity, p = mv; a vector quantity.
The product of average force and time interval, J = FΔt; equal to the change in momentum.
The impulse on an object equals its change in momentum: FΔt = Δp.
The total momentum of a system stays constant when no net external force acts on it.
A system with no net external force acting on it.
A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy decreases.
A collision in which the objects stick together, losing the maximum kinetic energy consistent with momentum conservation.
The backward motion of an object when it pushes another object forward, as momentum stays zero overall.
The point that moves as if all the system's mass were concentrated there.
A force exerted by one part of a system on another part; internal forces don't change total momentum.
A force exerted on the system by something outside it; it can change total momentum.
A plot of force against time; the area under it is the impulse.

practice.stem: What is the momentum of a 3 kg ball moving at 4 m/s?

distractors.A: Computed mv² = 48 and halved it: that's kinetic energy.

practice.stem: A 50 N average force acts on a ball for 0.2 s. What impulse does it deliver?
The total momentum of a system is conserved when

choices.text: all objects move at the same speed
the net external force on the system is zero

practice.explanation: Only external forces can change a system's total momentum.

distractors.B: Momentum is conserved in inelastic collisions too.
distractors.D: Sticking is one kind of collision, not the condition for conservation.

practice.stem: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the colliding objects

choices.text: stick together and move with a common velocity
bounce apart with no loss of kinetic energy
reverse direction with the same speed

practice.explanation: "Perfectly inelastic" means the objects stick; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy decreases.

distractors.C: Momentum is conserved in an isolated collision.

practice.stem: A 2 kg cart moving at 6 m/s collides with a 4 kg cart at rest on a frictionless track. The carts stick together. What is their velocity after the collision?
In a crash, an airbag reduces injury to a passenger mainly because it

choices.text: reduces the passenger's change in momentum
increases the time over which the passenger's momentum changes, reducing the average force
increases the impulse on the passenger

practice.explanation: The passenger's Δp is fixed (moving to stopped). Spreading it over more time lowers F = Δp/Δt.

distractors.C: Impulse equals Δp, which is unchanged.
distractors.A: The passenger still goes from moving to stopped.

practice.stem: A billiard ball moving at speed v collides head-on, elastically, with an identical ball at rest. What happens immediately after the collision?

choices.text: The first ball stops and the second moves at speed v.
Both balls move at v/2 in the original direction.
The first ball bounces back at speed v and the second stays at rest.
Both balls move at v in the original direction.

practice.explanation: For equal masses, conserving both momentum and kinetic energy requires the velocities to exchange.

distractors.B: Conserves momentum but loses half the kinetic energy: that's perfectly inelastic.

practice.stem: A 0.5 kg ball at rest is struck by a force that rises linearly from 0 to 100 N and falls back to 0 over a total of 0.04 s (a triangular force-time graph). What is the ball's speed afterward?
practice.explanation: Impulse = triangle area = ½(0.04)(100) = 2 N·s. v = 2/0.5 = 4 m/s.

distractors.C: Reported the impulse as the speed.
distractors.A: Used the rectangle 100 × 0.04, forgetting the ½.

practice.stem: A 10 kg object at rest explodes into two pieces. A 4 kg piece moves right at 6 m/s. What is the velocity of the 6 kg piece?
practice.explanation: Total momentum stays 0: 4(6) + 6v = 0, so v = −4 m/s.

distractors.B: Lost the sign; momentum would no longer be zero.

practice.stem: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds straight back at 10 m/s. What is the magnitude of the ball's change in momentum?
practice.explanation: Taking toward the wall as positive: Δp = 0.2(−10) − 0.2(10) = −4 kg·m/s.

distractors.A: That's the change if the ball had stopped.

practice.stem: A 2 kg cart moving at 6 m/s collides with and sticks to a 4 kg cart at rest. How much kinetic energy is converted to other forms?
practice.explanation: K before = ½(2)(36) = 36 J. Final speed 2 m/s, so K after = ½(6)(4) = 12 J. Lost: 24 J.

practice.stem: A 2 kg puck moves right at 3 m/s and a 1 kg puck moves left at 3 m/s on frictionless ice. What is the velocity of the system's center of mass after they collide?

choices.text: It depends on whether the collision is elastic.

practice.explanation: v_cm = (2·3 + 1·(−3))/3 = 1 m/s right. With no external force, it's the same after any collision.

distractors.D: Collision type affects the individual velocities, not v_cm.

practice.stem: Two identical balls are thrown at the same speed at identical blocks resting on frictionless ice. Ball 1 sticks to its block. Ball 2 bounces straight back. Which block moves faster afterward?

choices.text: The block hit by ball 1, because the ball's mass is added to the block.
The block hit by ball 2, because the bouncing ball's momentum changes more, so it delivers more impulse.
Both move at the same speed, because both balls had the same momentum.
The block hit by ball 1, because a sticking collision transfers all kinetic energy.

practice.explanation: The impulse on the block equals minus the ball's Δp. A bouncing ball reverses direction, so its |Δp| exceeds that of a ball that just stops; the block receives more momentum.

distractors.D: Sticking collisions lose the most kinetic energy.
distractors.A: Even ignoring the combined velocity, the block alone gets less momentum when the ball sticks.

practice.stem: A 60 kg skater stands at rest on frictionless ice and throws a 2 kg ball horizontally at 15 m/s. What is the skater's speed afterward?

distractors.C: Reported the ball's momentum as a speed.

practice.prompt: Students want to test whether momentum is conserved when two carts collide and stick together on a horizontal track. Available equipment: two carts with Velcro bumpers, a set of masses to add to the carts, an electronic balance, two motion sensors, and a meterstick.
practice.stimulus:
Results from four trials:

| Trial | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total momentum before (kg·m/s) | 0.60 | 0.80 | 1.00 | 1.20 |
| Total momentum after (kg·m/s) | 0.58 | 0.77 | 0.97 | 1.16 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure the students could use to collect the data needed. Include what measurements are taken and how.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: On axes of momentum after (vertical) versus momentum before (horizontal), plot the data and draw a best-fit line. (Describe your graph.)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Use your best-fit line to evaluate whether momentum is conserved. Explain.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Identify one physical cause for the small difference between momentum before and after, and explain how it causes the difference.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: If the carts bounced apart instead of sticking, would the slope of the best-fit line be expected to change? Explain.

rubric.description: Measure each cart's mass (with any added masses) on the balance.
Use motion sensors to measure the moving cart's velocity just before and the combined velocity just after the collision.
Repeat with different masses or initial speeds to get a range of momenta.
Four points plotted correctly on labeled axes with units.
A straight line through the data, close to the origin.
A slope close to 1 means momentum after ≈ momentum before; momentum is approximately conserved.
Friction between the carts' wheels and the track (or air resistance).
Friction is an external force that exerts a small backward impulse, slightly reducing the system's momentum.
No; momentum is conserved in elastic and inelastic collisions alike, so the slope should still be about 1.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Measure the mass of each cart, including any added masses, with the electronic balance. Place a motion sensor at each end of the track. Push cart A toward cart B, which is at rest, and record cart A's velocity just before the collision and the combined carts' velocity just after. Calculate total momentum before (m_A v_A) and after ((m_A + m_B)v′). Repeat several times, changing the added mass or push speed, to get a range of values.

(b) The graph has momentum before (kg·m/s) on the horizontal axis from 0 to 1.4 and momentum after (kg·m/s) on the vertical axis from 0 to 1.4. The four points lie nearly on a straight line passing close to the origin.

(c) The slope of the best-fit line is about (1.16 − 0.58)/(1.20 − 0.60) ≈ 0.97. Since this is very close to 1, momentum after is nearly equal to momentum before: momentum is approximately conserved.

(d) Friction between the wheels and the track acts on the carts from outside the system. It exerts a small impulse opposite the motion during and just after the collision, slightly reducing total momentum, so p_after is a little less than p_before.

(e) No. Momentum is conserved in all collisions when external forces are negligible, whether the carts stick or bounce. Only kinetic energy would differ. The slope should still be close to 1.
